rationale: TDBRAIN recordings have had no artifact rejection, so eye blinks, movement bursts and electrode pops (worse in EO) inflate the mean-averaged Welch PSD, mostly in delta/theta. That noise blurs the theta/beta-type differences we want to pick up. This round switches Welch to median averaging across segments (scipy's bias-corrected median), which gives a PSD that ignores transient artifact segments. It also keeps everything else the same so this is the only change being tested.

I'm making the spectral estimate robust. I re-reference each recording to the common average and switch Welch from mean to median across segments. The mean lets a few artifact segments (blinks, movement, electrode pops) dominate the band powers, and the median stops that. The common average also removes recording-reference effects, so the same features should hold up on external clinics' data.

The recordings are raw, with no artifact rejection, so a few high-amplitude epochs (blinks, movement, electrode pops) can dominate the mean-averaged Welch PSD. I'm switching to a robust spectral estimate: re-reference each recording to the common average, then take the median across Welch segments instead of the mean. This should make the relative band powers, including the theta/beta information, reflect the typical background EEG rather than artifacts. It should also hold up better against reference and amplifier differences in the external datasets.

The recordings have no artifact rejection (eye blinks, muscle and movement bursts), and the original reference makes the topographies depend on the reference site. This change re-references each recording to the common average and uses median-averaged Welch PSDs, so short artifact bursts don't inflate band power. Relative power stays insensitive to amplitude scale, and the result should be cleaner theta/beta and alpha maps that also transfer to other amplifiers and references.

The recordings have no artifact rejection, so blinks, movement and electrode pops inflate the mean Welch PSD. This change uses a median across Welch segments (robust to artifacts) and an average re-reference first (more robust to differing original references), so the band powers reflect brain activity better and should hold up across clinics and amplifiers.

The recordings have no artifact rejection, so eye blinks, movement and muscle bursts (especially frontal delta in eyes-open and gamma bursts) can dominate a mean-averaged Welch PSD. This change uses median averaging across 2 s segments instead, which ignores those short transients. The goal is cleaner, scale-robust relative band-power estimates (theta, beta and the rest) without touching the rest of the pipeline. I haven't run it, so I don't have a Dev score yet.

The recordings have no artifact rejection, so blinks, eye movements and muscle bursts in a few windows inflate the delta and gamma power in the mean-averaged Welch PSD, especially in eyes-open. This change switches Welch to median averaging over 2 s segments with 50% overlap. That is a robust estimate that ignores outlier windows, which should give cleaner theta/beta-related relative power per subject. It also holds up across recording lengths and the external amplifiers.

The recordings are only minimally processed: no artifact rejection, the original reference, and possibly line noise. Eye blinks and movement bursts inflate the mean-averaged Welch spectrum, mostly in delta and theta, which is exactly where the ADHD theta/beta signal lives. This change re-references each recording to the common average and averages the Welch segments by median instead of mean, so short artifacts are suppressed and the band-power features stop depending on the amplifier's reference. That should also help on the external datasets. I have not run this; the harness will give the new Dev score.

These recordings have no artifact rejection. In the current solution, Welch averages the spectra of all windows with a mean, so a few blinks, movements or electrode pops can inflate delta and gamma power, especially in eyes-open. I'm switching the Welch PSD to a median across windows. This keeps the background spectrum (theta, alpha, beta) that relative power is meant to measure, it's insensitive to recording length, and the features and classifier stay the same.

I'm adding the aperiodic (1/f) exponent for each channel and condition. It is fitted on the log-log Welch PSD over 2–40 Hz, leaving out the 7–14 Hz alpha peak. ADHD has been linked to a changed excitation/inhibition balance that shows up as a flatter or steeper aperiodic slope, and that slope also confounds the theta/beta ratio, so giving the model the slope separately from relative band power should add signal. The exponent doesn't change with amplitude scale, which helps on external datasets.

The recordings have no artifact rejection and keep their original reference. I'm re-referencing each recording to the common average and switching Welch to median averaging across 2-s segments, so that bursts like blinks, movement and electrode pops no longer push up the averaged spectrum. This should make the relative band powers more reliable and less tied to the original reference, which also matters for the external datasets.

I'm making the spectral estimate robust to artifacts and to the recording reference, both of which differ across clinics. Before computing relative band power, each recording is re-referenced to the common average. Welch then takes the median over 2 s segments instead of the mean, so a few high-amplitude segments (blinks, movement, electrode pops) no longer dominate the per-subject band powers. The hypothesis is that this lowers per-subject noise in the theta/alpha/beta relative powers that carry the ADHD signal, and that it should hold up on external datasets with a different reference.

The recordings are raw, so eye blinks, movement and electrode pops add large transient power that the mean-averaged Welch PSD mixes into the delta/theta bands. That can hide the theta/beta differences we are looking for in ADHD. This version takes the median across 2-s Welch segments instead of the mean, which ignores artifact-heavy segments without dropping any data. Everything else stays the same. I have not run it, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

I'm making one preprocessing change: re-reference each recording to the common average, and estimate the Welch PSD with the median across 2-s segments instead of the mean. The recordings have no artifact rejection, so with the mean a few blinks or movement bursts can dominate the delta/theta and gamma power estimates; the median is much less sensitive to them. The common average also removes the original reference montage, which matters because the final champion is applied to external clinics with different setups. The theta/beta and alpha contrasts that carry the ADHD signal should then be measured more cleanly and should transfer better.

These recordings have no artifact rejection, and the default mean-averaged Welch PSD lets a few blink, movement or EMG bursts dominate the delta, theta and gamma estimates. Switching to median averaging across Welch segments makes the per-channel spectra robust to these transients, which should make the relative band power (and so the theta/beta information) a cleaner signal. Nothing else changes.

TDBRAIN recordings get no artifact rejection, so a few eye-blink, movement or EMG segments can dominate the mean-averaged Welch PSD and distort relative band power, especially delta, theta and gamma. This change takes the median across 2 s Welch segments instead of the mean. That gives a robust spectral estimate that ignores sparse artifact epochs while keeping the same feature set and classifier, so any change in score comes from cleaner spectral features.

I'm changing only how the spectrum is estimated; the features and classifier stay the same. Re-referencing to the common average makes relative band power independent of each recording's original reference. Median-averaged Welch segments stop eye blinks, movement bursts and other large artifacts from dominating the spectrum. Together these should give cleaner theta/alpha/beta estimates, which should help both the dev score and how well the model carries over to external EC-only datasets recorded with other references and amplifiers.

Switch the Welch PSD from mean to median averaging over 2-s segments. Recordings have had no artifact rejection, and blinks and movement bursts inflate delta and theta power. Children with ADHD likely move more, so this could produce theta/beta differences that are really artifacts. A median spectrum should give a cleaner and more transferable estimate of the background EEG rhythm. I haven't run this yet, so its effect on the dev score is unknown.

The recordings are raw (no artifact rejection, original reference). Blinks and movement inflate delta/theta power and blur the theta/beta signal, so this round makes the spectrum more robust in one step: re-reference each recording to the common average, then use Welch with a median instead of a mean across the 2-s segments, which down-weights segments with transient artifacts. The relative band-power features and the logistic-regression model stay the same, so any score change comes from the cleaner spectrum.

I'm adding one feature per channel and condition: the aperiodic (1/f) exponent, a robust least-squares fit of log-power against log-frequency over 2–40 Hz that excludes the 7–14 Hz alpha range. It tracks the cortical excitation/inhibition balance, which reportedly differs in ADHD. Relative band powers can't separate a broad spectral tilt from narrowband oscillations, which also confounds the theta/beta marker. The exponent doesn't depend on recording amplitude, so it should hold up on external datasets.
